paragraphs: Separating an object from its background does not explain how the object is divided into parts. This paper extends the Shape Boltzmann Machine, a model of foreground and background shape, to represent those internal divisions. The resulting Multinomial Shape Boltzmann Machine models the shapes of an object's parts rather than treating its foreground as a single undifferentiated region.

The model captures both local and global statistics of part shapes. This allows its representation to account for small-scale shape patterns as well as broader organization across the object. The authors combine that shape representation with an appearance model, producing a generative model of object images. Segmentation then becomes a probabilistic inference problem: the model is used to infer how an observed image should be divided into parts.

The authors evaluate the approach on two challenging datasets with substantial variation in shape and appearance. They report performance comparable to the state of the art. The contribution is therefore a unified probabilistic approach to part segmentation, with reported results showing that its combined shape and appearance representation can handle considerable visual variability.
neurips-2012-a-generative-model-for-part.tldr: A generative model combines object-part shapes and appearance to infer segmentations with results comparable to the state of the art.

paragraphs: Count models describe how often events occur, while mixture models describe observations through combinations of hidden components. This paper connects these seemingly separate approaches through negative binomial processes. Its central technique is data augmentation tailored to the negative binomial distribution: introducing additional hidden quantities that make the models easier to analyze and support efficient Gibbs sampling inference.

The authors develop fundamental properties of this framework and establish a specific connection to hierarchical Dirichlet processes. Normalizing a gamma–negative binomial process reduces it to a hierarchical Dirichlet process. This relationship places the two constructions within a common account and helps explain the theoretical, structural, and computational advantages discussed for the negative binomial formulation.

The paper also constructs several negative binomial processes with different mechanisms for sharing information and applies them to topic modeling. These models connect to existing algorithms while offering distinct ways to organize shared components. The stated findings emphasize that inference should address both the negative binomial dispersion and probability parameters, rather than leaving either parameter outside the learning process.
neurips-2012-augment-and-conquer-negativ.tldr: Negative binomial data augmentation unifies count and mixture models and enables efficient inference for models with different sharing mechanisms.

paragraphs: The cocktail party problem asks how to separate speech from a mixture of competing sounds. This paper treats separation as a structured classification task. It divides the mixture into time-frequency units and predicts speech dominance within each unit. The decisions are connected through a conditional random field, allowing the system to account for the temporal dynamics of speech.

Deep neural networks learn both the state and transition feature functions used by the conditional random field. The state functions help relate the input to individual classification decisions, while the transition functions support relationships between decisions over time. Learning both kinds of functions gives the structured model a way to represent complex, nonlinear relationships between the sound mixture and its desired output.

The classification formulation also allows direct optimization of a measure that correlates well with human speech intelligibility. That connects the learning objective to how understandable separated speech is, although correlation does not make the measure identical to intelligibility. The authors report substantial improvements over existing systems across a variety of noises, supporting the combination of learned nonlinear features and temporal structure.
neurips-2012-cocktail-party-processing-v.tldr: Deep neural networks and conditional random fields jointly predict speech dominance, improving separation across a variety of noises.

paragraphs: Exploration in reinforcement learning gathers information through actions, but those actions can incur costs as well as deliver rewards. This paper studies Bayesian reinforcement learning under that distinction. The learner seeks high expected long-term total reward while keeping its expected total cost within a constraint. Exploration must therefore be evaluated in terms of both what it teaches and what it costs.

The authors formalize the environment as a constrained Markov decision process. Its cost function provides a way to encode requirements on exploration, making those requirements part of the learning problem. They then extend BEETLE, a model-based Bayesian reinforcement learning method, so it can learn in environments with these cost constraints.

Simulated problems demonstrate the resulting cost-sensitive exploration behavior. The contribution is a formulation and method for learning when information-gathering actions must respect an expected cost budget. The expectation qualification matters: the stated constraint concerns expected total cost, rather than a guarantee that every individual sequence of actions stays below a fixed expenditure.
neurips-2012-cost-sensitive-exploration-.tldr: An extension of BEETLE learns to explore for long-term reward while accounting for constraints on expected total action cost.

paragraphs: Margin bounds help explain classification performance through how confidently examples are separated. Familiar bounds for support vector machines and boosting do not depend on feature-space dimension, which helps explain their usefulness in very large feature spaces. This paper asks whether dimension independence is unavoidable, or whether explicitly accounting for dimension can produce a tighter guarantee.

The authors prove a PAC-Bayes margin bound that increases with dimension when all other factors remain fixed. For finite-dimensional feature spaces, it is strictly sharper than a particular established dimension-independent PAC-Bayes margin bound. As dimension tends to infinity, the two bounds approach equivalence. The result therefore identifies a finite-dimensional improvement while retaining a connection to the earlier guarantee.

Under mild conditions, the new bound also recovers the VC bound for linear classifiers. Experiments on benchmark datasets find that it is useful for model selection and substantially sharper than both comparison bounds. These findings concern the informativeness of the guarantee; its increasing dependence on dimension does not by itself assert that actual classification performance must worsen whenever dimension grows.
neurips-2012-dimensionality-dependent-pa.tldr: A dimension-dependent PAC-Bayes margin bound tightens an established bound in finite-dimensional feature spaces and proves useful for model selection.

paragraphs: A changing signal can have sparse differences between successive observations even when its full representation is more complicated. This paper uses that structure to recover sequences of vectors from linear measurements. It assumes that each increment has a limited number of nonzero entries and allows the measurement matrix and noise to vary across the sequence.

The proposed convex program minimizes a weighted sum of the absolute values of successive differences while enforcing the measurement constraints. In the noiseless case, the authors prove exact recovery when each measurement matrix satisfies a restricted isometry condition of an order depending only on its corresponding increment sparsity. This is notable because the equivalent aggregate compressive-sensing matrix does not satisfy the usual restricted isometry requirements.

For bounded measurement noise, the authors introduce a quadratically constrained recovery program and derive reconstruction-error bounds. Simulations and an application to real video data provide additional support. The result shows how analyzing the individual measurement matrices and temporal differences can establish recovery guarantees that a standard analysis of the aggregate matrix would not supply.
neurips-2012-exact-and-stable-recovery-o.tldr: Minimizing sparse temporal differences enables exact noiseless recovery under per-measurement matrix conditions and bounded-error recovery with bounded noise.

paragraphs: This paper addresses learning sparse representations in linear models when the noise level is unknown. It considers fused sparsity, where the sparse structure being learned is organized through linked quantities rather than simply treating every model component independently. The task combines recovering that structure with handling uncertainty about the amount of noise in the observations.

The authors propose the Scaled Fused Dantzig Selector, or SFDS. They formulate its learning problem as a second-order cone program, giving the estimator a concrete optimization-based implementation. This formulation is the central algorithmic contribution: it provides a way to approach fused sparse estimation without requiring the noise level to be known in advance.

The paper places particular emphasis on a fused-sparsity instance involving outliers, connecting the method to robust estimation. It establishes finite-sample risk bounds and evaluates the approach on synthetic and real data. The bounds provide theoretical control for estimation with a finite dataset, while the experiments examine the method in practice. Together, these contributions address structured sparsity and unknown noise within one estimation framework.
neurips-2012-fused-sparsity-and-robust-e.tldr: The Scaled Fused Dantzig Selector estimates fused sparse linear models with unknown noise levels, including a setting involving outliers.

paragraphs: Image denoising removes unwanted corruption, while inpainting reconstructs image regions that need repair. This paper combines sparse coding with deep networks pretrained using denoising autoencoders. Its main methodological change is an alternative training scheme that adapts denoising autoencoders from unsupervised feature learning to these image restoration tasks.

A central application is blind inpainting, where the region requiring repair is not supplied beforehand. The authors demonstrate removal of complex superimposed patterns, including text, extending beyond the simpler case of pixels missing at random. The approach therefore handles a setting in which the restoration system must operate without an externally provided map of the damaged region.

Experiments support the method's effectiveness for both denoising and blind inpainting, with state-of-the-art performance reported for denoising. The authors also find that their revised autoencoder training scheme is more effective for unsupervised feature learning. The contribution thus connects a change in representation training to practical restoration capabilities, including the stated ability to remove structured corruption without advance knowledge of its location.
neurips-2012-image-denoising-and-inpaint.tldr: A revised denoising-autoencoder training scheme supports strong image denoising and removal of structured corruption without a supplied repair mask.

paragraphs: Matrices often come with documents describing their rows or columns. This paper develops a model that analyzes both sources together. A focused topic model represents each document through hidden binary features indicating topics, while a new matrix decomposition assigns binary features to rows or columns and imposes a low-rank constraint.

The two models are connected by sharing their binary feature vectors. This gives the text analysis and matrix decomposition a common representation, so the documents participate directly in how the matrix is modeled. The low-rank constraint adds structure to the matrix component, while the shared topic features establish the link between textual content and matrix patterns.

The authors apply the method to roll-call voting data, using legislation as the associated text. They report state-of-the-art prediction of votes on new legislation using only its observed text. This is a meaningful use of the coupling: text can support predictions for legislation whose votes are not yet available. The authors also show that the connection to legislative text helps explain properties of the learned matrix decomposition.
neurips-2012-joint-modeling-of-a-matrix-.tldr: Shared binary topic features connect documents to a low-rank matrix model, enabling vote prediction for new legislation from its text.

paragraphs: Training very large neural networks requires methods that can use substantial computing resources effectively. This paper introduces DistBelief, a software framework designed to train models with billions of parameters across clusters containing thousands of machines and tens of thousands of CPU cores. It addresses both the scale of trainable models and the speed of training.

The framework includes two distributed optimization approaches. Downpour SGD uses asynchronous stochastic gradient descent with many model replicas. Sandblaster supports distributed batch optimization, including an implementation of L-BFGS. These provide different ways to distribute the work of updating model parameters, and the authors report that both Downpour SGD and Sandblaster L-BFGS improve training scale and speed.

The system trains a network reported as 100 times larger than previously described in the literature and achieves state-of-the-art ImageNet performance on a task containing 16 million images and 21,000 categories. The same techniques also substantially accelerate a smaller network used for commercial speech recognition. Although the reported applications concern neural networks, the authors describe the underlying algorithms as applicable to gradient-based machine learning more broadly.
neurips-2012-large-scale-distributed-dee.tldr: DistBelief distributes neural-network optimization across large computing clusters, enabling much larger models and faster training.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much computation is needed to learn a classifier with error close to the best margin-based halfspace. Its target error is at most (1 + alpha) times the optimal gamma-margin error, plus epsilon. Smaller alpha asks for a tighter multiplicative comparison. Learning is improper, meaning the output classifier need not itself be a halfspace.

The known endpoints leave a substantial gap. At alpha = 1/gamma, hinge-loss methods achieve polynomial time and sample complexity. At alpha = 0, the cited prior result rules out time polynomial in 1/gamma, while an exponential-time approach is possible. The paper investigates intermediate alpha values to understand how relaxing accuracy changes computational requirements.

The authors derive positive results connecting these endpoints. In particular, they identify cases where alpha grows more slowly than 1/gamma and learning still takes polynomial time. This shows that polynomial-time learning can sometimes achieve a stronger error comparison than the stated hinge-loss endpoint. The results also extend to adversarial online learning and PAC learning with malicious noise.
neurips-2012-learning-halfspaces-with-th.tldr: New learning guarantees identify intermediate accuracy targets that can improve on the hinge-loss error comparison while remaining polynomial-time in some cases.

paragraphs: Detecting distributional change means identifying when the statistical pattern generating observations has shifted. This paper develops a generalized Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for that problem in high-dimensional data. The method is nonparametric, so the proposed testing approach does not depend on choosing a particular parametric family to describe the distributions being compared.

To implement the test, the authors introduce a hierarchical estimator of minimum-volume sets. These sets provide a representation of the distributions through regions where observations are concentrated. Rather than making distribution representation a separate preliminary issue, the paper develops an estimator specifically as part of the testing method. The hierarchical construction is a central component of the proposed approach.

The motivating setting is detecting changes in data streams, where observations continue to arrive and testing efficiency matters. The authors state that their test is especially efficient in this context. They provide theoretical foundations and report superiority over existing methods. The contribution combines a high-dimensional statistical test with a distribution representation designed to make that test practical for change detection.
neurips-2012-learning-high-density-regio.tldr: A generalized nonparametric Kolmogorov-Smirnov test uses hierarchical high-density region estimates to detect changes in high-dimensional data streams.

paragraphs: Manually sorting friends into social circles takes effort, and those groups need updating as a personal network grows. This paper turns circle discovery into a machine learning task. It analyzes a user's ego-network, specifically the network of connections among that user's friends, and treats circles as groups of nodes to be learned.

The proposed model combines friendship connections with information in user profiles. For each circle, it learns both who belongs and a circle-specific measure of profile similarity. This allows different groups to be associated with different patterns of similarity. Membership is not restricted to a single circle, enabling the model to represent overlapping groups and groups nested within larger ones.

The authors evaluate the approach using data from Facebook, Google+, and Twitter, with hand-labeled circles serving as ground truth for each source. They report accurate circle identification across this diverse collection. The findings support using network structure together with profile information, while the membership formulation makes the resulting organization capable of reflecting more than one social grouping for the same person.
neurips-2012-learning-to-discover-social.tldr: A model combines friendship links and profile information to discover social circles that can overlap or nest within one another.

paragraphs: Linear support vector machines are useful for recognition, but good performance can require high-dimensional features. Deep representations offer another route, although training multilayer perceptrons involves difficult nonconvex optimization. This paper proposes a deep nonlinear classifier built from layers of linear support vector machines, using random projections to connect successive layers.

Each layer computes weak predictions, and a random projection of those predictions recursively transforms the data representation for further learning. The complete construction is nonlinear even though its layers use linear SVMs. The authors state that the method scales like linear SVMs and requires neither kernel computations nor nonconvex optimization, connecting a layered representation with comparatively straightforward learning components.

The paper reports better generalization than kernel-based SVMs, especially when training examples are fewer than input dimensions. Experiments on several vision and speech benchmarks show consistent improvements over previous methods and identify random projections as a key ingredient. These findings support the recursive construction as a practical way to learn nonlinear classifiers in the evaluated settings, particularly where dimensionality is high relative to sample size.
neurips-2012-learning-with-recursive-per.tldr: Layers of linear SVMs connected by random projections form a nonlinear classifier with reported improvements on vision and speech benchmarks.

paragraphs: Predicting links in a changing graph can draw on how graph-level or node-level features evolve over time. This paper assumes that selected features, such as node degree, follow a vector autoregressive model. In this formulation, past feature values inform future ones, and the authors propose using that temporal structure to improve link prediction.

The method jointly optimizes adjacency matrices, which represent connections, and the matrices governing the autoregressive feature model. It accounts for both sparsity and low rank in these matrices. Joint estimation brings the predicted network and its modeled feature dynamics into the same optimization problem, rather than handling the two as unrelated estimates.

The authors derive oracle inequalities that describe trade-offs in choosing smoothing parameters when sparsity and low rank act together. These theoretical results help characterize the effects of balancing the two structural properties. They also provide an efficient computation method using proximal optimization through a generalized forward-backward algorithm. The contribution combines a stated temporal modeling assumption, structured matrix estimation, and a practical optimization procedure.
neurips-2012-link-prediction-in-graphs-w.tldr: Joint estimation of graph connections and autoregressive feature dynamics combines sparsity and low rank for time-evolving link prediction.

paragraphs: Finding the most likely configuration in a chain or tree can be done exactly with dynamic programming. However, the computation grows quadratically with variable domain size, making large sets of possible labels expensive. This paper identifies wasted effort in scoring hypotheses that already have strong negative local evidence, while noting that beam-search alternatives sacrifice exactness.

The authors introduce exact inference algorithms combining column generation with precomputed bounds on the model's cost structure. The approach uses that structure to reduce computation in typical cases. It does not improve the worst-case performance, which the abstract states cannot be improved, but it retains exact inference while targeting the inefficiencies encountered in practical problems.

Experiments report twice the speed of exact Viterbi for Wall Street Journal part-of-speech tagging and more than thirteen times the speed for joint part-of-speech tagging and named-entity recognition. The approach also extends to approximate inference and faster two-best inference. The central finding is that exactness can be preserved alongside substantial practical speedups, even when worst-case complexity remains unchanged.
neurips-2012-map-inference-in-chains-usi.tldr: Column generation and cost bounds accelerate exact inference in chains and trees in practice without improving worst-case complexity.

paragraphs: Some systems occupy discrete states but change state at times that can occur anywhere along a continuous timeline. This paper studies inference for such systems when their trajectories consist of jumps between states. It proposes an exact Markov chain Monte Carlo framework that connects continuous-time trajectories with computations performed on a sampled discretization of time.

The sampler alternates between two conditional steps. First, it samples a random time discretization given the current trajectory, using properties of the Poisson process to do so efficiently. Second, it samples a new trajectory given that discretization. This second step can use discrete-time MCMC techniques based on the forward-backward algorithm.

The discretization is therefore part of the sampling procedure and changes with the trajectory. That construction allows the authors to retain an exact MCMC formulation while using discrete-time computational tools. They compare their approach with particle MCMC and a uniformization-based sampler and report advantages. The main contribution is a simple alternating framework that makes established discrete-time inference techniques useful for continuous-time jump systems.
neurips-2012-mcmc-for-continuous-time-di.tldr: An exact MCMC sampler alternates random time discretizations and trajectories to infer continuous-time systems with discrete states.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model sets in which diversity matters. Although operations such as normalization and sampling are tractable, finding the most probable set is NP-hard. Greedy methods have had empirical success, but their existing approximation guarantees apply only to the special case of monotone kernels. This paper develops an alternative for a broader non-monotone setting.

The method uses continuous optimization for submodular maximization. Its key ingredient is a new continuous relaxation of the DPP log-probability function that can be evaluated and differentiated exactly and efficiently. This distinguishes it from the multilinear extension used for general submodular functions and makes the relaxation useful as the basis of a practical inference algorithm.

The authors establish a one-quarter approximation guarantee for a general class of non-monotone DPPs. The method also extends to complex polytope constraints, allowing combinations with models such as Markov random fields and weighted matchings. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show better performance than greedy methods. The contribution combines a broader guarantee with a computationally accessible relaxation and support for structured constraints.
neurips-2012-near-optimal-map-inference-.tldr: A tractable continuous relaxation supports approximate DPP MAP inference with a one-quarter guarantee for a general class of non-monotone models.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many observations a particular robust subspace recovery method needs to estimate its target accurately. The analysis focuses on a robust estimator of a generalized inverse covariance matrix, used within a convex robust PCA algorithm. Its assumptions include independent, identically distributed observations from an underlying sub-Gaussian distribution.

The main result bounds the estimation error with high probability at order N^(-0.5 + epsilon), for arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The choice of epsilon affects the probability estimate. This convergence rate approaches the N^(-0.5) rate associated with direct covariance and inverse covariance estimation, giving a quantitative comparison between this robust estimator and familiar matrix estimators.

In some natural settings, the probability bound yields Frobenius-norm sample complexity of order D^(2 + delta), for arbitrarily small positive delta, compared with D² for direct covariance estimation. Similar convergence and sample-complexity results follow for the corresponding robust subspace recovery algorithm. The findings show rates close to those of PCA under the stated assumptions, rather than establishing identical requirements for every robust PCA method.
neurips-2012-on-the-sample-complexity-of.tldr: Under i.i.d. sub-Gaussian sampling, a particular robust PCA method has convergence and sample-complexity rates close to those of ordinary PCA.

paragraphs: Some network models process both present and missing edges, making each approximate inference iteration require at least quadratic time in the number of nodes. This paper proposes representing a network through triangular motifs instead. A motif here is a triple of vertices containing either two or three edges, so the representation includes more than complete triangles.

The number of motifs scales with the sum of squared node degrees. For networks with low maximum degree, that quantity is much smaller than the square of the node count. The authors use this representation to build a mixed-membership network model and approximate inference algorithm. For high-maximum-degree networks, they propose node-centered motif subsampling, trading a small reported accuracy cost for faster inference.

Experiments show faster runtime and improved mixed-membership community detection accuracy compared with an edge-based model. The paper also demonstrates the approach on a network of approximately 280,000 nodes. The benefit depends on degree structure or subsampling: changing the representation reduces the computational burden in the stated settings while retaining useful information for community inference.
neurips-2012-on-triangular-versus-edge-r.tldr: Representing networks with two- and three-edge triangular motifs enables faster mixed-membership inference, particularly for networks with low maximum degree.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion aims to reconstruct a matrix from incomplete observations using its low-rank structure. This paper develops gradient methods on a Grassmann manifold, a space used to represent subspaces. Its central change is a scaled metric, which changes the geometry used to determine gradient updates during the search for a suitable low-rank completion.

The proposed scaling significantly improves canonical gradient methods, with especially strong benefits reported for ill-conditioned matrices. The authors state that the methods maintain established global convergence and exact recovery guarantees. Thus, the contribution improves the optimization procedure while preserving the theoretical guarantees available in the relevant setting, rather than asserting recovery for arbitrary incomplete matrices.

The paper also establishes a connection between scaled gradient descent and a form of subspace iteration for matrix completion. Building on the scaled gradient, the authors propose a conjugate gradient method that outperforms several existing algorithms and is competitive with recently proposed alternatives. These results connect a geometric change in the optimization method with improved practical performance and a relationship to another subspace-based procedure.
neurips-2012-scaled-gradients-on-grassma.tldr: Scaled Grassmann-manifold gradients improve low-rank matrix completion, especially for ill-conditioned matrices, while retaining established guarantees.

paragraphs: Weighted automata can represent functions that assign real numbers to strings, supporting tasks in text, speech, and computational biology. Earlier spectral learning methods addressed a narrower setting: learning a probability distribution from samples drawn from that same distribution. This paper extends the approach to general weighted automata when samples come from an arbitrary distribution.

The central obstacle is missing information in the Hankel matrix used by spectral learning. The authors address it through constrained matrix completion, then combine the completed matrix with the spectral method. This produces a family of learning algorithms that connects recovery of missing matrix entries with construction of a weighted automaton.

For one algorithm in that family, the authors establish generalization bounds. Their proofs analyze the stability of matrix completion and spectral learning together, accounting for the combined procedure rather than treating either component alone. The result broadens the sampling setup supported by spectral automaton learning and supplies a theoretical guarantee for a particular member of the proposed family.
neurips-2012-spectral-learning-of-genera.tldr: Constrained matrix completion extends spectral weighted-automaton learning to samples from arbitrary distributions, with generalization bounds for one resulting algorithm.

paragraphs: In Go/NoGo tasks, choosing Go ends a trial immediately, while choosing NoGo requires waiting until a deadline. Participants show a Go bias, with both more hits and more false alarms. This paper proposes that the bias can arise from a strategic response to unequal time costs, rather than requiring differences in sensory processing between Go/NoGo and two-alternative forced-choice tasks.

The authors derive a Bayesian decision policy that balances errors against average decision delay. It naturally produces the observed Go bias and is equivalent to a drift-diffusion model with a threshold that first rises and later collapses near the deadline. The initial rise reflects the diminishing time advantage of choosing Go as the trial proceeds.

Fitting a simpler fixed-threshold model to this policy reproduces the previously observed higher threshold for Go/NoGo than forced-choice decisions. However, that approximation cannot reproduce the Go bias itself. The findings offer a possible explanation for apparent differences between the tasks: rational adjustment to their cost structures may suffice, without implying additional underlying sensory or cognitive differences.
neurips-2012-strategic-impatience-in-go-.tldr: A decision policy balancing errors and delay explains how Go bias may arise rationally from the unequal time costs of Go and NoGo responses.

paragraphs: A graphical model represents patterns of conditional independence among variables. This paper investigates whether those patterns can be read from the nonzero entries of an inverse generalized covariance matrix for discrete variables. Such a relationship was already established for multivariate Gaussian models, but its significance outside the Gaussian setting was an open question addressed by this work.

The authors show that, for certain graph structures, the inverse covariance matrix of vertex indicator variables reflects the graph's conditional independence structure. Indicator variables encode discrete outcomes in a form suitable for covariance calculations. The restriction to particular graph structures is essential to the stated result; the paper does not claim the relationship for every discrete graphical model.

Using these population-level results, the authors show how graphical Lasso can recover edges for certain classes of discrete models. Simulations provide supporting verification of the theory. The contribution connects a matrix-based representation of statistical dependence to graph recovery beyond Gaussian distributions, while identifying a setting in which an established estimation tool can be used for discrete data.
neurips-2012-structure-estimation-for-di.tldr: For certain discrete graphical models, inverse covariance structure reveals conditional independences and supports edge recovery with graphical Lasso.

paragraphs: Some statistical questions depend on how frequently values occur, without depending on the names of those values. For observations drawn independently from one distribution, the data profile records the multiset of occurrence counts. This paper studies distributions over such profiles, motivated by label-invariant problems in areas including population estimation, text classification, and speech recognition.

The quantity of interest is minimax KL divergence, which has several interpretations. In compression it measures unavoidable additional coding cost beyond entropy. In sequential prediction it describes the smallest achievable worst-case expected log-loss regret. It also provides an upper bound on how many distributions can be distinguished in hypothesis testing, linking the same mathematical quantity to several tasks.

For profiles generated by length-n i.i.d. sequences, the authors bound redundancy between 0.3 times n^(1/3) and n^(1/3) times log₂ n. These bounds improve previous results and establish the exact power of n governing growth. The remaining logarithmic gap means the result fixes the growth exponent without making the upper and lower bounds identical.
neurips-2012-tight-bounds-on-profile-red.tldr: New bounds establish a one-third growth exponent for profile redundancy, connecting label-invariant data to compression, prediction, and distinguishability.
